notes:
I've written up Psalm 88 below, but there are gaps. My search tools hit their limit before I could open several pages I'd planned on, including the NET Bible notes, Gill, Ellicott's full chapter, Lutheran and Orthodox sources, and anything on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. So those are missing, and a few verses (12, 16, 17) have thin notes.

**Overview**
- The psalm is often called the darkest psalm. Its author is Heman, a man whose life seems by all accounts to have been blessed.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Keil & Delitzsch (an older German commentary) say the faint spark of faith never goes out, yet the gloom never turns into hope. the Psalm dies away in Job-like lamentation https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-88.html
- Sam Storms: some have suggested Psalm 89 continues Psalm 88 to give it a happier ending, but there is little evidence to support this theory. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/darkness--my-only-companion--psalm-88-

**v. 1**
- Guzik: "God of my salvation" looks back to past rescue and holds on to future hope. He calls it one of the psalm's few glimmers of light. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Guzik quotes the Puritan John Trapp: in the early church this psalm was sung as a public confession by people who had been excommunicated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Reformed (TGC, Bert Daniel): simply continuing to pray when life seems hopeless is itself evidence of God's grace. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-saddest-psalm-in-scripture/
- Catholic (Augustine): he reads the whole psalm as the voice of Christ praying. "Day" means good times and "night" means disaster. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the prayer is passionate and constant. It is a loud cry for help, not a shout of joy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Augustine: a prayer "entering" God's presence means God accepts it. God "inclining his ear" means he listens with compassion, since God has no body. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm

**v. 3**
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): … actually, Spurgeon's line is: "Trouble in the soul is the soul of trouble." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Pulpit Commentary: "grave" is literally Sheol, the place of departed spirits. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-88.html
- Augustine compares this verse to Jesus saying "My soul is sorrowful, even unto death." Christ's soul could be full of human evils, though not of human sins. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: other people already expected him to die. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Methodist (Timothy Tennent, Seedbed): the early church linked Psalms 22, 69 and 88 with Christ's sufferings. One reason was that this psalm describes someone on the edge of death. https://seedbed.com/darkness-is-my-closest-friend-psalm-88/
- Augustine: "pit" means the depth of misery or of hell. People who thought Christ died like any other man counted him among those going down to the pit. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm

**v. 5** (older versions read "free among the dead")
- Benson/Barnes (older commentaries collected on Bible Hub): the dead are "free" from life's burdens, but the psalmist takes no comfort from that idea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/88-5.htm
- The Geneva Bible notes say "cut off from your hand" means God's care, which is meant according to the judgment of the flesh. In other words, it describes how things feel, not how they are. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/88-5.htm
- Pulpit: he is laid among corpses like an unburied man, as in a battlefield pit where some are not yet dead. Earlier psalms say the dead do not remember God; here, God does not remember the dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-88.html
- Guzik: it is wrong to read this as proof that there is no life after death. The Old Testament understanding of the afterlife is shadowy, and Christ brought it to light. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Augustine: "free among the dead" points to Christ, the only sinless one among sinners, who laid down his life freely. He reads "whom you remember no more" as "not yet," meaning the dead whose resurrection has not yet come. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: the affliction comes straight from God's hand. https://biblehub.com/psalms/88-6.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes: seeing God behind it is not blame-shifting but faith. They also link the darkness to the darkness at the crucifixion. https://biblehub.com/psalms/88-6.htm
- Augustine: "the lowest pit" is the deepest misery there is. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik: he does not protest that God's wrath is unfair, and shows a deep sense of his own sin. On "Selah," Guzik quotes Spurgeon: a swimmer lifting his head between waves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- TGC (Daniel): the repeated "you… your" shows the psalmist still believes God is in control, and that is a sign of hope. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-saddest-psalm-in-scripture/

**v. 8**
- Guzik, quoting Maclaren: the words may point to a loathsome disease such as leprosy, possibly as a picture of affliction in general. VanGemeren links it to the disciples abandoning Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Keil & Delitzsch: the word means close friends, not mere acquaintances. He is alone in a prison of misery he cannot escape. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-88.html
- Storms: like many of us, Heman reads his distress as a sign that God may have abandoned him. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/darkness--my-only-companion--psalm-88-

**v. 9**
- Guzik: raised hands were the familiar Hebrew posture of prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Augustine struggled with what "eyes grow dim" could mean if applied to Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: this is not about the final resurrection, since that hope had hardly yet dawned on Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/88-10.htm
- Matthew Henry: souls that have died may praise God, but dead bodies cannot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/88-10.htm
- Pulpit: "departed spirits" translates *rephaim*, the faint, shadowy dead in Sheol. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-88.html
- Constable: these questions do not contradict teaching about conscious life after death. They show Heman wanted to praise God on this side of the grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/88-10.html
- Do traditions differ here? StudyLight lists Trapp (Calvinist) and Wesley (Arminian) next to each other. Both read the verse as "raised in this world," and Clarke (Wesleyan) reads "any more in this life?" On this verse I found agreement, not a real split. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/88-10.html
- Bible Hub: taken as a whole, the Bible answers "yes": there will be praise after the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/psalms/88-10.htm
- Augustine: he takes "the dead" mainly as people spiritually dead in heart, whom even Christ's miracles do not wake to faith. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm

**v. 11**
- Spurgeon: if God let his servant die before keeping his promise, no one could proclaim his faithfulness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps088.cfm
- Augustine: Scripture likes to pair loving-kindness with faithfulness, and "destruction" (Abaddon) repeats the idea of "the grave." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801088.htm
- Bible.org: the psalm uses a series of names for the afterlife. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-88

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: "the land of forgetfulness" is another name for Hades or Sheol. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-88.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: if he died, he could neither receive God's wonders nor praise him for them. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-88.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik, quoting Matthew Poole: even without an answer so far, he will not stop praying or hoping. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: his worst affliction is feeling cast off by God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- TGC (Daniel): without a felt sense of God's love, a believer may fear that death only brings more misery. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-saddest-psalm-in-scripture/

**v. 15**
- Storms: Heman's suffering has lasted his whole life. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/darkness--my-only-companion--psalm-88-
- Guzik: even here he calls them "Your terrors," which shows a crisis of faith, not unbelief. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/

**v. 16**
- Spurgeon: God's terrors made him feel like a leper. But this is the sufferer's impression, and not the very truth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps088.cfm

**v. 17**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the burnings of wrath become floods, since God's wrath can be pictured as any destroying element. They number this verse 18, following the Hebrew. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-88.html

**v. 18**
- Guzik: the NIV's "darkness is my closest friend" can mean that, in a real sense, the darkness has been a friend. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-88/
- Tennent (Methodist): this is the only psalm that ends on such a dark note. Even so, it calls on God's covenant name four times, and from Augustine onward the church linked it with Christ's suffering. https://seedbed.com/darkness-is-my-closest-friend-psalm-88/
- TGC (Daniel, Reformed): real faith can exist even when we feel worse after praying. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-saddest-psalm-in-scripture/
- TGC (Christina Fox, Reformed): Jesus faced the darkness of the grave so believers could be called friends of God. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/how-i-gleaned-hope-from-the-darkest-psalm/
- Coffman: the saddest part is that he feels God has not even heard him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/88-18.html

**Notes on traditions**
Every Protestant source I read agrees on the main points: the faith is real, the despair is honest, Old Testament knowledge of the afterlife was limited, and the psalm points to Christ. The only clearly different approach is Augustine's. He reads the whole psalm as Christ speaking, and some verses (like v. 10) as about spiritual death. I found no material on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm.
